parts: Please read the manuscript within /papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/recurrence, and consider the most recent work as well. I want to spend some time understanding the current results. Can you summarize the results, making sure to include the lowest level rungs of the hierarchy as explicitly as possible, and then explaining how the higher order terms are determined through recurrence formulas, be them algebraic, differential, or something different.
I’ll read the manuscript and recent notes, then lay out the first few rungs explicitly and explain how the recurrences generate the higher terms.

The hierarchy has two parts: curvature corrections to the arithmetic modes, and a Riemann–Siegel correction retained as a heat integral. The current manuscript matches their orders to obtain a proved error bound. I’m checking the latest notes too, especially the distinction between the analytical accuracy result and the evaluator that remains to be built.

The first two frozen levels give errors \(X^{-7/4}\) and \(X^{-11/4}\), measured relative to the gamma scale. Each new level combines higher derivatives of the gamma factor with products of lower derivatives. Gaussian moments turn those polynomials into explicit heat solutions, so generating the terms requires no new differential equation at each order.

I can now give the first three rungs explicitly. There are three useful recurrence formulas: one for the curvature polynomials, one for their Gaussian moments, and one for the Riemann–Siegel coefficients. I’ll also keep the two error scales distinct, since the newest accuracy result is relative to the smaller outer envelope.

The current manuscript gives a **systematic finite hierarchy of approximations to the negative-time Riemann heat flow**. Its terms are explicit: gamma derivatives supply the coefficients, algebraic recurrences assemble them, and Gaussian moments evolve them in time. A separate Riemann–Siegel correction must improve alongside the hierarchy.

I read the [manuscript](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/recurrence/manuscript/main.tex), its recent integration assessment, and the current research register. The central results are:

- For each fixed order \(p\ge1\), the error is \(O(X^{-(p+3/4)})\) relative to the gamma scale, including three spatial derivatives and one time derivative.
- A separate argument permits \(p\) to grow with \(\log X\), giving much stronger accuracy relative to the smaller outer envelope.
- Recent work establishes quadrature and evaluation-error budgets. The certified evaluator remains under development.

Here is how the construction works, starting from its lowest rungs.

The exact field is
\[
h(T,z)=H(-T,z),\qquad
h_T=h_{zz},\qquad
h(0,z)=\frac18\xi\!\left(\frac{1+iz}{2}\right).
\]
Thus \(T>0\) corresponds to negative original time. It has the exact representation
\[
h(T,z)=\int_{\mathbb R}k_T(z-u)H(0,u)\,du,
\qquad
k_T(v)=\frac{e^{-v^2/(4T)}}{\sqrt{4\pi T}}.
\]
This normalization agrees with the classical [Polymath heat-flow formulation](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438).

Fix a large real center \(X\), and write
\[
d=z-X,\qquad q=u-X,\qquad
L=\log\frac{X}{4\pi},\qquad
N=\left\lfloor\sqrt{\frac{X}{4\pi}}\right\rfloor.
\]
The construction keeps **every arithmetic mode \(1\le n\le N\)** and both conjugate arms. The center, cutoff, coefficients and integration endpoints stay fixed when differentiating in \(z\) or \(T\).

For an arm \(\epsilon=\pm1\), define
\[
w_\epsilon(z)=\frac{1+\epsilon iz}{2},\qquad
M(w)=\frac{w(w-1)}{16}\pi^{-w/2}\Gamma(w/2),
\qquad
\ell_\epsilon(z)=\log M(w_\epsilon(z)).
\]
The arithmetic mode at initial time is
\[
M(w_\epsilon(z))n^{-w_\epsilon(z)}.
\]
Its local form is especially useful:
\[
M(w_\epsilon(X+q))n^{-w_\epsilon(X+q)}
=b_{\epsilon n}e^{\lambda_{\epsilon n}q}A_\epsilon(q),
\]
where
\[
b_{\epsilon n}=M(w_\epsilon(X))n^{-w_\epsilon(X)},\qquad
\lambda_{\epsilon n}=\ell_\epsilon'(X)-\frac{\epsilon i}{2}\log n,
\]
and
\[
A_\epsilon(q)
=\exp\left(\sum_{r\ge1}c_{\epsilon r}q^{r+1}\right),
\qquad
c_{\epsilon r}=\frac{\ell_\epsilon^{(r+1)}(X)}{(r+1)!}.
\]

The arithmetic index \(n\) changes the amplitude and slope. **All modes in one arm share the same curvature coefficients \(c_{\epsilon r}\).** Those coefficients are exact gamma derivatives, with simultaneous bounds of the form
\[
|c_{\epsilon r}|\le AD^{r-1}X^{-r}.
\]

Suppress the arm label temporarily. The first coefficients are
\[
c_1=\frac{\ell''(X)}2,\qquad
c_2=\frac{\ell'''(X)}6,\qquad
c_3=\frac{\ell^{(4)}(X)}{24}.
\]
The hierarchy groups products by their suggested power of \(X^{-1}\):
\[
\begin{aligned}
a_0(q)&=1,\\
a_1(q)&=c_1q^2,\\
a_2(q)&=c_2q^3+\frac12c_1^2q^4,\\
a_3(q)&=c_3q^4+c_1c_2q^5+\frac16c_1^3q^6.
\end{aligned}
\]
The order-\(p\) initial polynomial is
\[
P_p(q)=a_0(q)+\cdots+a_p(q).
\]

This grading matters. The term \(c_1^2q^4/2\) belongs to level two because \(c_1^2=O(X^{-2})\); the term \(c_3q^4\) belongs to level three because \(c_3=O(X^{-3})\). Ordinary polynomial degree would put both at the same degree.

All subsequent levels follow from the **algebraic recurrence**
\[
\boxed{
a_0=1,\qquad
j\,a_j(q)=\sum_{r=1}^{j}r\,c_rq^{r+1}a_{j-r}(q).
}
\]
It comes from introducing a bookkeeping parameter \(s\):
\[
\exp\left(\sum_{r\ge1}c_rq^{r+1}s^r\right)
=\sum_{j\ge0}a_j(q)s^j,
\]
then differentiating with respect to \(s\). Thus every partition of the chosen weight is included automatically. Adding only the next gamma derivative would omit necessary products of earlier derivatives.

The heat evolution of these polynomials is explicit too. Put
\[
\mu=d+2T\lambda.
\]
Then
\[
\int_{\mathbb R}k_T(d-q)e^{\lambda q}q^m\,dq
=e^{\lambda d+T\lambda^2}\mathcal H_m(\mu,T),
\]
where
\[
\mathcal H_m(\mu,T)
=m!\sum_{\nu=0}^{\lfloor m/2\rfloor}
\frac{T^\nu\mu^{m-2\nu}}{\nu!(m-2\nu)!}.
\]
The lowest moments are
\[
\begin{aligned}
\mathcal H_0&=1,\\
\mathcal H_1&=\mu,\\
\mathcal H_2&=\mu^2+2T,\\
\mathcal H_3&=\mu^3+6T\mu,\\
\mathcal H_4&=\mu^4+12T\mu^2+12T^2.
\end{aligned}
\]
Higher moments obey the simple recurrence
\[
\boxed{
\mathcal H_m=\mu\mathcal H_{m-1}
+2T(m-1)\mathcal H_{m-2}.
}
\]

Consequently, for **one arithmetic mode**, the first evolved contributions are
\[
\begin{aligned}
u_0&=be^{\lambda d+T\lambda^2},\\[2mm]
u_1&=be^{\lambda d+T\lambda^2}
\,c_1(\mu^2+2T),\\[2mm]
u_2&=be^{\lambda d+T\lambda^2}
\left[
c_2(\mu^3+6T\mu)
+\frac{c_1^2}{2}(\mu^4+12T\mu^2+12T^2)
\right],\\[2mm]
u_3&=be^{\lambda d+T\lambda^2}
\left[
c_3\mathcal H_4+c_1c_2\mathcal H_5
+\frac{c_1^3}{6}\mathcal H_6
\right].
\end{aligned}
\]
Here \(u_j\) denotes the new contribution at level \(j\); the approximation through level two uses \(u_0+u_1+u_2\).

For example, the complete first-level expression for one mode is
\[
\boxed{
be^{\lambda d+T\lambda^2}
\left[1+\frac{\ell''(X)}2
\bigl((d+2T\lambda)^2+2T\bigr)\right].
}
\]
At the chart center \(d=0\), its bracket becomes
\[
1+\ell''(X)\bigl(T+2T^2\lambda^2\bigr).
\]

There is also an equivalent **differential-operator recurrence**. Define
\[
\mathcal Q_T=d+2T\partial_d,
\qquad
U_{\epsilon,j}=\sum_{n=1}^{N}u_{\epsilon n,j}.
\]
Then
\[
U_{\epsilon,0}
=\sum_{n=1}^{N}b_{\epsilon n}
e^{\lambda_{\epsilon n}d+T\lambda_{\epsilon n}^2},
\]
and
\[
\boxed{
jU_{\epsilon,j}
=\sum_{r=1}^{j}
r\,c_{\epsilon r}\mathcal Q_T^{\,r+1}U_{\epsilon,j-r}.
}
\]
In particular,
\[
\begin{aligned}
U_{\epsilon,1}
&=c_{\epsilon1}\mathcal Q_T^2U_{\epsilon,0},\\
U_{\epsilon,2}
&=\left(c_{\epsilon2}\mathcal Q_T^3
+\frac{c_{\epsilon1}^2}{2}\mathcal Q_T^4\right)U_{\epsilon,0}.
\end{aligned}
\]
These are two representations of the same construction: one evaluates Gaussian moment polynomials; the other applies powers of \(\mathcal Q_T\). Neither requires solving a new differential equation at each level. The [hierarchy section](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/recurrence/manuscript/sections/03_hierarchy.tex) derives their equivalence.

The arithmetic hierarchy needs its **Riemann–Siegel completion**. The actual finite model is
\[
\boxed{
F^{[p,K]}(T,z)
=\sum_{\epsilon=\pm1}\sum_{j=0}^{p}U_{\epsilon,j}(T,z-X)
+\mathcal I_{X,K,B}(T,z).
}
\]
On a fixed interval \(\tau\le T\le B\), the retained integral is
\[
\mathcal I_{X,K,B}
=\int_{X-V_B}^{X+V_B}k_T(z-u)
\bigl[S_{m(u)}(u)-S_N(u)+R_{m(u),K}(u)\bigr]\,du,
\]
where
\[
V_B=8\sqrt{\max(1,B)}\,L,\qquad
m(u)=\left\lfloor\sqrt{\frac{u}{4\pi}}\right\rfloor,
\]
and \(S_m\) is the exact gamma-mode sum through \(m\).

The difference \(S_{m(u)}-S_N\) pays for the change between the natural cutoff at \(u\) and the frozen chart cutoff. The remaining term is
\[
R_{m,K}(u)=2\Re\left[
(-1)^{m-1}M(w_+(u))\mathcal U(u)a(u)^{-1/2}
\sum_{k=0}^{K}C_k(\chi(u),1/2)a(u)^{-k}
\right],
\]
with
\[
a(u)=\sqrt{\frac{u}{4\pi}},\qquad
\chi(u)=1-2(a(u)-m),
\]
\[
\mathcal U(u)=
\exp\left[-i\left(
\frac u4\log\frac{u}{4\pi}-\frac u4-\frac{\pi}{8}
\right)\right].
\]

The \(C_k\) have their own recurrence construction. In the manuscript’s complex normalization,
\[
F_0(\chi)=
\frac{e^{\pi i(\chi^2/2+3/8)}
-i\sqrt2\cos(\pi\chi/2)}
{2\cos(\pi\chi)},
\]
with apparent singularities filled analytically. Expanding the coefficient recurrence gives
\[
\begin{aligned}
C_0&=F_0,\\
C_1&=\frac{F_0^{(3)}}{12\pi^2},\\
C_2&=\frac{F_0^{(6)}}{288\pi^4}
+\frac{F_0^{(2)}}{16\pi^2}
-\frac{iF_0}{96\pi}.
\end{aligned}
\]
More generally,
\[
C_k=\pi^{-2k}
\sum_{j=0}^{\lfloor3k/2\rfloor}
\left(\frac{\pi}{2i}\right)^j
\frac{e_j^{(k)}}{(3k-2j)!}
F_0^{(3k-2j)}.
\]
Starting from \(e_0^{(0)}=1\), the rational weights obey, for \(m=3k-2j>0\),
\[
e_j^{(k)}
=\frac{(m-1)(m-2)}4e_j^{(k-1)}
-e_{j-2}^{(k-1)},
\]
with out-of-range entries zero and the first term absent for \(m=1,2\). For positive even \(k\), the final entry is
\[
e_{3k/2}^{(k)}
=-\sum_{h=1}^{3k/2}\frac{(-1)^h}{h!}
e_{3k/2-h}^{(k)}.
\]
These identities come from the [Arias de Reyna coefficient formulas](https://arxiv.org/html/2201.00342v1). Thus the completion combines derivatives of one explicit entire function with recursively generated rational weights.

The two orders match at
\[
\boxed{K=2p.}
\]
The reason is visible in the errors. The omitted curvature terms begin at \(X^{-(p+1)}\), while summing the complete arithmetic population contributes an allowance \(X^{1/4}\). Their combined error is therefore \(X^{-(p+3/4)}\). The retained Riemann–Siegel expansion has remainder allowance \(X^{-(K/2+3/4)}\). Choosing \(K=2p\) balances them.

The resulting comparison is:

| Approximation | Arithmetic content | RS coefficients retained | Gamma-scale error |
|---|---|---|---|
| Earlier elementary short formula | All modes, elementary carriers | Leading correction | \(O(X^{-3/4})\) |
| Earlier target-dependent first correction | Exact gamma modes, first curvature correction | \(C_0,C_1\) | \(O(X^{-5/4})\) |
| Frozen \(p=1\) | \(U_0+U_1\) | \(C_0,C_1,C_2\) | \(O(X^{-7/4})\) |
| Frozen \(p=2\) | \(U_0+U_1+U_2\) | \(C_0,\ldots,C_4\) | \(O(X^{-11/4})\) |
| Frozen \(p=3\) | \(U_0+\cdots+U_3\) | \(C_0,\ldots,C_6\) | \(O(X^{-15/4})\) |
| Fixed \(p\ge1\) | \(U_0+\cdots+U_p\) | \(C_0,\ldots,C_{2p}\) | \(O(X^{-(p+3/4)})\) |

Here the gamma scale is
\[
G(z)=\sqrt{M(w_+(z))M(w_-(z))}.
\]
The bounds control
\[
\frac{
\max_{0\le j\le3}|\partial_z^j(h-F)|
+|\partial_T(h-F)|
}{|G(z)|}
\]
uniformly on fixed complex charts and fixed compact intervals \(0<\tau\le T\le B<\infty\), after a sufficiently large onset.

Every frozen finite model also satisfies
\[
(\partial_T-\partial_z^2)F^{[p,K]}=0
\]
**exactly**. Its approximation error comes from its initial-data approximation and localization. The earlier target-dependent first correction agrees with the frozen first correction at the chart center, but has different spatial derivatives and a nonzero heat residual. The [comparison section](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/recurrence/manuscript/sections/04_comparison.tex) explains this distinction.

The most recent analytical advance concerns **growing order**. A fixed algebraic error relative to \(G\) does not establish accuracy relative to the smaller outer envelope: conversion can cost \(e^{L^2/8}\) on \(1\le T\le2\).

[Note05](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/recurrence/notes/05_CONTROLLED_ORDER_GROWTH_AUDIT_20261026.md) separately bounds the order-dependent constants, whose logarithms grow like \(O(p\log p)\). It proves that
\[
p=\lfloor L/2\rfloor,\qquad K=2p
\]
gives
\[
\boxed{
\|h-F^{[p,2p]}\|_{\mathrm{outer}}^{(3,1)}
\le e^{-L^2/4}
}
\]
eventually on \(1\le T\le2\). This retains all modes and the integral. It does not assert convergence of an infinite hierarchy.

[Note06](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/recurrence/notes/06_COEFFICIENT_ROUNDING_AND_RS_QUADRATURE_20261026.md) then proves sufficient evaluation-error budgets, including \(O(L^2)\) Gauss nodes per integration branch and requested normalized accuracy
\[
\frac{3L^2}{8\log2}+O(L\log L)
\quad\text{bits}.
\]
That is a conditional accuracy specification. The [current register](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/recurrence/research-progress/01_RECURRENCE_RESEARCH_PROGRESS_20261026.md) records the provider-algorithm audit as underway; no completed provider theorem was saved when I checked.

The results retain the status stated in the [heat-flow results index](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/result-summaries/11_newman_heat_flow_reductions_and_certificates.md): analytical proofs from named inputs, with internal LLM assessments. Independent specialist validation, useful computational onsets, and transfer to the physical observables remain outstanding. The [recorded separate-error cautions](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/avoid/12_term_by_term_matching_and_separate_bounds.md) explain why the arithmetic hierarchy, canonical completion and evaluation errors must continue to be controlled together.
What is the difficulty with extending it to larger values beyond negative time?
I’ll check the manuscript’s time restrictions and the earlier results through \(t=0\), so I can explain what changes as time becomes positive.

The finite recurrence formulas can be continued to positive time. The difficulty is carrying their error bounds with them: positive original time amplifies high frequencies and requires control of the initial approximation at complex arguments. Earlier work already crosses zero on a shrinking time window, so \(t=0\) is a boundary of the present estimates, not a singularity of the exact field.

Assuming you mean increasing the original time \(t\) through zero into \(t>0\), **the recurrence formulas extend readily; the difficulty is proving that their errors remain small.** The exact Riemann heat field itself exists on both sides of zero.

Recall that \(T=-t\). Negative original time gives the forward heat equation
\[
h_T=h_{zz},
\]
whereas increasing original time gives
\[
H_t=-H_{zz}.
\]
That change reverses the stability of approximation errors.

For example, an initial error \(\delta\cos(kz)\) evolves as
\[
\begin{array}{ll}
t=-T<0:&\delta e^{-Tk^2}\cos(kz),\\[2mm]
t>0:&\delta e^{tk^2}\cos(kz).
\end{array}
\]
Negative time suppresses high frequencies; positive time amplifies them. Consequently, a small initial error in the present real-axis norm does not by itself guarantee a small positive-time error. The canonical field has enough analytic structure to evolve, but we must preserve and quantify that structure in the approximation.

There are four concrete consequences for this hierarchy.

**First, its finite arithmetic terms are not the obstruction.** For example,
\[
be^{\lambda d+T\lambda^2}
\]
continues to
\[
be^{\lambda d-t\lambda^2},
\]
and the moment polynomials simply acquire \(T=-t\). Likewise, the operator becomes
\[
\mathcal Q_{-t}=d-2t\partial_d.
\]
The resulting finite arithmetic hierarchy still satisfies the correct evolution equation exactly. What does not follow automatically is its closeness to the canonical field.

**Second, the completion needs a different representation and stronger source estimates.** The negative-time proof uses a decaying Gaussian acting on *real* initial data:
\[
H(-T,z)=\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi T}}
\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-(z-u)^2/(4T)}H(0,u)\,du.
\]
Simply substituting \(T=-t\) destroys that decay. For positive time, the available identity instead samples complex arguments:
\[
H(t,z)=\frac1{\sqrt{4\pi t}}
\int_{\mathbb R}e^{-v^2/(4t)}H(0,z+iv)\,dv.
\]
This is the imaginary-direction Gaussian representation used in the [Polymath analysis](https://arxiv.org/html/1904.12438).

The present recurrence proof deliberately relies on a real Riemann–Siegel remainder theorem. Positive time requires an appropriate complex-domain remainder estimate, or a contour argument that pays for the shifted contours, connectors and tails. Analytic continuation of the **retained finite correction** does not supply such a bound for the **discarded remainder**.

**Third, the current estimates deteriorate near zero even though the exact field is regular there.** On complex charts, taking absolute values of the negative-time kernel produces factors such as
\[
e^{b^2/(4T)},\qquad T^{-1},\qquad T^{-2}.
\]
These prevent the existing compact-\(T\) theorem from being taken uniformly to \(T=0\). They reflect losses in that proof method.

Earlier work already handles this boundary by a different crossover approximation on
\[
|t|\log\frac{X}{4\pi}\le8.
\]
Thus crossing zero has been achieved at a weaker, separately proved accuracy. The remaining problem is extending the sharper recurrence estimates and matching them uniformly to positive-time estimates. See the [signed crossover result](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/notes/04_COMPLEX_STRIP_REMAINDER_AND_BUFFERED_CROSSOVER_20261025.md).

**Fourth, increasingly large positive times move the relevant saddle.** The current hierarchy expands gamma curvature about a frozen center \(X\). As positive time grows, the important complex displacement grows, and more curvature terms matter. Eventually a formula centered at the moving saddle becomes more suitable. The earlier manuscript retains an implicit gamma-saddle equation
\[
p_t(w)=w+\frac t2\,\alpha(p_t(w)),
\qquad \alpha=\frac{M'}M,
\]
for that purpose. Controlling it jointly in time and height is a separate task from extending to one fixed positive-time interval.

The repository therefore treats the next fixed positive interval, \(1/2\le t\le1\), as a bounded analytical task. Its [prepared request](/Users/ebbaker/Documents/shifted-zeta-positivity/papers/investigations-5/01_heat_density_asymptotics/ansatz/research-progress/handoffs/HDA-A08-AN01.md) asks for the missing canonical source, contour and derivative estimates. **There is no established impossibility here:** the immediate gap is a controlled positive-time comparison; much larger times additionally require adapting the saddle and proving uniform time–height bounds.

If you instead meant larger \(T=-t\), hence more negative original time, the fixed-order theorem already covers every fixed compact interval \(0<\tau\le T\le B<\infty\). What remains open there is uniform control as \(B\) itself grows with height.

I didn't realize that T was defined as negative t, is that redundant?

To fix the understanding, when you say T or t, which one is related to the De Bruijn Newman time?
I’ll check the normalization against the standard de Bruijn–Newman convention, so the sign and any scaling are explicit.

**Lowercase \(t\) is the standard de Bruijn–Newman time.** There is no additional rescaling in this manuscript.

It appears in
\[
H(t,z)=\int_0^\infty e^{tv^2}\Phi(v)\cos(zv)\,dv,
\qquad H_t=-H_{zz}.
\]
The de Bruijn–Newman constant \(\Lambda\) is the threshold such that all zeros of \(H(t,\cdot)\) are real precisely when \(t\ge\Lambda\). This is the convention used by [Rodgers and Tao](https://arxiv.org/abs/1801.05914).

**Uppercase \(T=-t\) is an auxiliary variable introduced for studying negative de Bruijn–Newman times.** It contains no additional information:

| De Bruijn–Newman time \(t\) | Auxiliary \(T=-t\) |
|---|---|
| \(-2\) | \(2\) |
| \(-1\) | \(1\) |
| \(0\) | \(0\) |
| \(+1\) | \(-1\) |

Its purpose is to write
\[
h(T,z)=H(-T,z),\qquad h_T=h_{zz},
\]
so the negative-time problem takes the familiar forward heat-equation form with \(T>0\).

So yes, it is redundant as a parameter, but convenient for the Gaussian calculations. Increasing \(T\) means **decreasing de Bruijn–Newman time**.

In particular, the recurrence result stated on \(1\le T\le2\) concerns
\[
\boxed{-2\le t\le-1}
\]
in standard de Bruijn–Newman time.

I’ll use **lowercase \(t\) as the primary time variable** in our discussion, and explicitly identify \(T=-t\) whenever translating a manuscript formula.
